Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Dominion Succession Duty Act and to provide:
1. That rates of tax upon or in respect of any succession upon the death of a person after December 31, 1946, shall be twice the rates presently in force and that the tax paid to the government of any province in respect of the same succession be allowed as a deduction from the tax payable under the Dominion Succession Duty Act up to but not exceeding one-half of the tax otherwise payable under the said act.
Succession Duty Act

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Stanstead had just asked a question, and I am not sure that I remember it exactly; if I am wrong he will correct me. In a province in which the succession duty rate is as high or higher than the present dominion rate, this legislation will not increase the liability of the taxpayer. That is obvious because he is entitled to deduct up to fifty per cent of the dominion rate. In cases where the provincial rate is 50 per cent or greater, then a little exercise in mathematics will show that there is no increased liability. In the province in which there are no succession duties, or where the duties are up to one-half the present dominion rates, then unquestionably the tax liability of estates would be increased when this law comes into effect over the present combined dominion and provincial rate.

I do not want to review or revive the controversy that we had earlier in tire session, but it seems to me that in a province like Quebec, which derives a substantial revenue from succession duties, a heavy burden will be placed upon the people if there is failure to retire from the field of succession duties. That is what prompted my question.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The burden is not greater;
it will remain exactly the same.

The burden which was
assumed is an incident of the war. Quebec is now asked to retreat from the field which has yielded a very substantial proportion of the income of that province. I will not say there has been a threat, but if a province is wilful and continues in the exercise of its constitutional right to collect succession duty it will suffer as compared with the more submissive province that yields up its right to that tax.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No, I should not think so; I think the result would be just the opposite. I think it would continue to be in exactly the same position. The more submissive province which yields up its right to levy on the taxpayer in that province will continue to be in approximately the same position. The only difference will be that the province referred to by my hon. friend as the submissive province will receive the succession duties through arrangement with the dominion instead of collecting succession duties directly through its own succession duties department. That is the only difference I can see.

When the minister says a province will receive the succession duties through the dominion does he mean it will receive a sum by reason

of its having given up that duty, or does he mean it will in fact receive the succession duties collected for it by the dominion?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The province will have
rented its right to collect succession duties and will be paid a sum in lieu of that right, as well as of others.

Could the minister give
the figures which would show the present duties exigible, say on an estate of 150,000, where a man leaves a widow and two children, breaking it up into dominion and province of Quebec rates?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I have not the figures for
a man leaving a widow and two children, but where a man leaves a widow with an estate of $50,000 the present dominion tax would be $1,470 and the provincial tax would be $2,000. The combined tax is $3,470, and under the proposed legislation there will be no change in the total reported.
Could' the minister give the same information for Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not happen to have it on $50,000 for Ontario, but I have it for $60,000.
Take $60,000, and give it also for Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Well, for some reason or another they have not $60,000 for Quebec.
Have you some figure common to all the provinces which will help?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I have given $50,000, so perhaps I had better stick to that. I have already given it for Quebec. In Ontario the provincial tax is $1,438 compared with $2,000 in Quebec; the dominion tax is $1,470, and1 the total tax $2,908. No change under the proposed legislation.
There would be, I think, a slight increase there, where the Ontario duty is a little lower than the dominion.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: In that case, I am informed, there would be perhaps $12 or $14 difference, the Ontario duty being somewhat less than the dominion duty-actually, $32 less. If my hon. friend is interested in comparative figures I will put them all on. All this is contained in the volume entitled "Succession Duties", a reference book to the dominion-provincial conference on reconstruction, table 2, page 24.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: On $50,000 in Saskatchewan the provincial tax is $1,375, the dominion $1,470, a total tax of $2,845. There would be a small increase in that bracket-a difference of $95, I am informed-in Saskatchewan.

And Prince Edward
Island?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Prince Edward Island:
provincial tax $3,750, dominion tax $1,470, a combined tax of $5,220. No change.
What is New Brunswick?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: New Brunswick: provincial tax $2,200, dominion tax $1,470, total $3,670. No change.
Would the minister give the figures for Manitoba?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Manitoba: provincial tax $1,725, dominion tax $1,470. No change. I have given the figures for Ontario. Alberta: provincial tax $1,800, dominion tax $1,470, total $3,270. No change. British Columbia: provincial tax $563, dominion tax $1,470, total tax $2,033. Increased tsx, $907.
You see, Mr. Chairman, that shows the unfairness of this provision so far as British Columbia is concerned; it is highway robbery.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: My hon. friend seems to have a sympathetic audience behind him.

I would refer the Acting Minister of Finance to the budget speech, Hansard, page 2910, where the Minister of Finance used these words:
. . . the general burden of the combined dominion and provincial succession duties in those provinces which continue to levy succession duties will be the same as at present.
In other words, he gave the assurance that if a province did not come into this agreement the citizens of that province would not have to pay increased succession duties by reason of the change in the Dominion Succession Duty Act. Yet you have this change brought in by the government, which, in the case the minister has just mentioned, makes a difference of $900, double the amount of the provincial tax. I suggest that that situation could be met by inserting a proviso to the effect that succession duty levied by the dominion under this doubling of succession duty tax is not to be increased in a nonagreeing province; in other words, that there is to be no increase in succession duty in a non-agreeing province.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I will take a note of my hon. friend's representation. He will observe that the minister in the statement said, the "general burden of the combined dominion and provincial succession duties." It varies, depending on the bracket and the rate.

But as I read that statement of the Minister of Finance it meant that the citizen of a province that did not agree was not to be discriminated against by reason of this change in the dominion succession duty law and he would not have to pay any increased tax.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: There is no distinction between provinces that agree and disagree so far as tax treatments are concerned.
There is, in -that very statement. It refers to provinces which do not agree.

Is that a complete
statement?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I make that as a positive statement:	there is no distinction made
between provinces which agree and which disagree so far as tax credit is concerned.

There is no complete agreement between the different provinces, and you find overlapping and double succession duty as between the provinces. A man who dies in Montreal owns stocks which are on a register in Edmonton, and Alberta collects duty on an asset which is subject to duty in Quebec. Now under the agreement which is held out that would disappear; it is an added enticement, possibly, to kneel down and adore.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not accept the phrase money.
Yes, kneel down and save money.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not accept the phrase, "kneel down."

Kneel down at that price. But I think the minister will admit that to that extent his statement was not all-embracing. I think that that does constitute an exception to the broad statement which he has made.

Can the minister indicate what the increased revenue would be to the dominion? As I see it, the only place in which the dominion will get anything additional as the matter stands is in provinces where the tax is less than the
Succession Duty Act

dominion tax. That is, where the tax is equal to the dominion tax the dominion doubles the tax and takes half of it off. How much more will the dominion get? I am puzzled to understand why this legislation was introduced at all. Is there specifically a benefit to the dominion treasury, or is there some other point of which I am not aware?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The figure of course would have to be based on the past year, because one cannot tell what the rates will be in the future. Assuming the number of deaths and the value of estates to be the same as last year, the total collectible by the dominion would be double, but it would have to give credit up to fifty per cent of its tax for the tax paid in the particular province in which the deceased was resident. I am advised by the deputy minister that the net result would be about the same, assuming that no province entered into the suggested agreement.

(Muskoka-Ontario)
When you say "the net result would be the same" you mean the dominion would get about the same as it does now?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes.
That is what I rather guessed. Then why this change in the legislation? Is it not a long way round to get to the same place?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: If a province agreed and went out of the succession duty field, in that province there would be only half the rate in force as compared with the other provinces, and one purpose of this is to endeavour to achieve reasonable equality of succession duty rates throughout Canada.

I am not sure that I follow the minister when he says half the rate. Does that mean that the dominion rate is so much less than the provincial rate that even doubling the dominion rate means that there will be only half as much as before?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Let us say that the dominion rate on an estate to-day would produce $1,500 and the provincial rate $1,500, or a total of $3,000. That is the present tax liability of the estate of a deceased, let us say, in the province of Quebec. The province of Quebec decides to come into the agreement and goes out of the succession duty field. If then the rate were not doubled the result would be that in the province of Quebec the succession duty liability would be restricted to $1,500, the dominion rate, whereas in Ontario, which for the purposes of our argument we

will assume has the same rate of tax, an estate of the same size would continue to pay $3,000.

That does not answer my question. That is supposing a state of affairs to exist which does not exist at all. As I see it, the dominion is putting into one pocket exactly what it takes out of the other. In other words by doubling the tax you are not going to alter the situation. There must be some other reason for this. If you are not going to get any more money, what are you getting?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am afraid I cannot follow my hon. friend's argument.
The minister said in answer to me a moment ago that the dominion government was going to get virtually the same sum by doubling the tax.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I qualified that; I said, "if" none of the provinces came into this agreement. If some come in, the dominion will obviously get more, and to those provinces the dominion will have to make the payments provided for in the agreement. If all the provinces come in, the dominion will get approximately double what it is getting to-day. If only some come in, it will get less than double.

Is there not another way of getting around the difficulty for a province that is in the position of British Columbia? Could you not say that there shall be no doubling of dominion succession duty except in a province which agrees to give up the levying of succession duty taxes?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I have promised to give consideration to the representations my hon. friend has made on that point. I should1 like to think them over.

A province that is relying upon succession duties for a big proportion of its revenue is more seriously affected by this proposal than a province that is not relying upon succession diuties to the same extent. For instance, where the duty on an estate of a given amount under Quebec law is $2,000, under British Columbia law the payment is only $500. So by yielding up succession duty Quebec suffers much more than does British Columbia or does any other province which has a low succession duty. Is that not a fact?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Not necessarily, because British Columbia may be relying for its total' revenue on other types of taxation.

Yes, on other types Which are not taken over by the federal government-

Income War Tax

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not know that that is the ease. It may be that British Columbia is getting a larger revenue from personal income tax and certain corporation taxes than was Quebec. As a matter of fact I think it does get a very muoh greater revenue from those sources. There is a quid pro quo all along the line.
In so far as the issues are before us, British Columbia would be in a much better position by yielding up succession duties than Quebec or Ontario would be.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I cannot agree.
Mr. HAiCKETT: On the estate that I referred to British Columbia would yield up but $500, whereas on an estate of an equal amount the province of Quebec would yield up $2,000.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is only one element in the revenues which the provinces are yielding.
The others are personal income and corporation tax.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Gasoline tax and the rest.
There you get into a field where theTe was not complete understanding. The minister based his offer on the three taxes just mentioned, personal income, corporation tax and succession duties.

Let me ask this question. Will the minister agree to these two propositions? First of all, having regard to the provinces that are likely to be adhering provinces, to use the minister's term, and to the amount of income which they have raised from succession duty, the amount which the dominion is likely to get by doubling this tax is comparatively trivial. Second, would not this provision be a very strong deterrent to a province raising a substantial amount of succession duty from increasing its succession duty rate any further?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Of course it is obvious that if a province is now levying a rate higher than the present dominion rate, this would be no deterrent because they are up already to the dominion rate.. It may be a deterrent to increasing rates still further.
That was my question. Would it not be a strong deterrent to a province increasing its rate? I want to be clear on that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
My answer is, no more
than there is to-day. If it is 56 per cent to-day, there is a deterrent to raising it to 60 per cent. If they raised it to 60 per cent there would still be a credit up to half of the dominion tax.
If the province should raise its rate, the rebate is half of the dominion tax, not half of its own.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
This resolution and succeeding resolutions up to No. 15 deal, broadly speaking, with the taxation of cooperatives. As hon. members are no doubt aware, numerous representations have been made by cooperative organizations regarding the budget proposals as they affect their operations. The government has considered these representations carefully, for it is anxious that the tax laws should not only be fair and equitable but workable. This, as hon. members are aware, is an extremely difficult and contentious field of taxation, and I doubt whether any legislation can be framed which will please everyone concerned. The best that can be hoped for is a reasonably equitable plan which preserves equity between various forms of enterprise. The government felt that the best way to arrive at this equitable plan was to appoint a representative commission to hear evidence and to bring in a report. This it did in 1944, and may I remind hon. members that this commission included a member nominated by the Cooperative Union of Canada, a member nominated by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, two impartial and
Income War Tax

highly regarded economists, and a judge. I do not think anyone could accuse this commission either of bias or of lack of competence.
To a very large degree the government has adhered to the commission's report. The report is not necessarily the final word on the subject, but unless the government is to take the view that the commission was incompetent or biased, I think it has every reason for giving the recommendations a fair trial.
Some of the representations received have, in effect, urged the government to reject the commission's main line of approach and enact legislation giving special exemptions to cooperatives generally. These could not be accepted. A number of representations have been made, however, which the government is able to accept without a major change of policy or without departing too far from the commission's recommendations. Two of these suggestions necessitate amendments to the resolution, and in a few moments I shall ask one of my colleagues to make the necessary motion. For example, certain cooperatives have pointed out that it is physically impossible for them to pay out patronage dividends within six months after the end of their fiscal years. Accordingly it is proposed to allow twelve months for such distributions. Certain other cooperatives find that the limitation with respect to payment of patronage dividends for years earlier than 1942 presents difficulties. This limitation was originally inserted because until 1941 very few cooperatives paid any tax whatever and were therefore free of tax on patronage dividends allocated but not paid. To give exemptions when these amounts are paid out would therefore result in a double benefit to the taxpayer. However, in view of alleged discrimination 'between cooperatives, some of which operate on a five-year revolving fund and some of which finance themselves out of a fund which revolves over a period longer than five years, the limitation is being withdrawn.
These are relatively minor changes. More important is the question whether patronage dividends should be deductible if paid at a different rate to members than to non-members. As my colleague the Minister of Finance pointed out, the government in framing its proposals on this point followed the recommendations of the McDougall commission. The commission was in unanimous agreement* that patronage dividends should be paid equally to members and non-members. I am emphasizing this because the impression seems to have been created that by proposing this rule the government was attempting to make it difficult for cooperatives to grow and enlarge their membership. Nothing could be further

from the truth. It is clear, however, that many cooperatives fear that the requirement of equal treatment for members and non-members would be prejudicial to their development. Since the government has no desire either to hamper the development of the cooperative movement or to appear to be hampering that development, it is willing to go a long way toward meeting this objection. In fact the government proposes to accept in principle a plan proposed by a great many of the cooperatives themselves. These cooperatives have suggested on many occasions that they should be free to make a distinction between members and non-members but should be required to pay tax on income derived from dealings with non-members. While this does not affect the resolution itself, which is in very general terms, I am taking this occasion to say that in the legislation founded on the resolution provision will be made whereby a cooperative which wishes to pay patronage dividends only to members, or at a lower rate to non-members, will be able to treat such patronage dividends as a deduction, provided that they pay tax on income arising from non-member business.
In order to anticipate any discussion there may be on the point, I should perhaps add that the proposed legislation will meet the case of certain cooperatives, such as the Alberta and Saskatchewan wheat pools, which wish to transfer certain outstanding obligations from inactive members to new and active members. Provision is already made, of course, for the continued operation of ordinary revolving funds.
So far as the resolutions affecting the future operation of the cooperatives are concerned, that is all. There is a question which has been raised by a number of hon. members in the course of the budget debate relating to what in my judgment has been inaccurately referred to as retroactive taxation. I refer, of course, to the assessments made against the western wheat pools for income tax during the years 1942 to 1945 inclusive. The committee will recall that in his budget speech the minister made an offer to the pools of settlement of these claims. Following the delivery of the budget speech the minister met the representatives of the pools and discussed the question with them. The members will recall that later the minister said that he had had this discussion, and that if it were felt by the pools that the proposed offer of settlement was not fair he was prepared to consider some further adjustment. Following the minister's departure I met the representatives of the pools on Monday. They submitted to me a counter-

Income War Tax
proposal for settlement of these claims. That counter-proposal is now under consideration by the government, and I simply want to say I am confident that a settlement will be arrived at which will be satisfactory to all concerned, but which, I must emphasize, must be fair to all those, including the general public, who are affected. I refrained from taking part in the budget debate chiefly because I wanted to feel justified in taking a little time to place my views before the committee on this very important question. When I gave way to the leader of the opposition a few minutes ago I hoped he would cover the subject so thoroughly that it would not be necessary for me to take very much time. I must confess that I was somehow disappointed in what I heard. The question which has been brought before the committee is one which requires looking into to a greater extent than simply changing the wording of the resolution, or the legislation which may follow. I say that because the whole question whether this government and future governments are going to take an appropriate altitude toward cooperative enterprise is at stake.
The resolution before us starts out by providing for the repeal of what are here described as certain provisions exempting the incomes of

certain cooperative companies. It does not name those provisions, although I imagine the reference is to section 4 (p) of the statute.
It is significant that that section was not mentioned either in the resolution or in the remarks of the Acting Minister of Finance. It provides for the repeal of that section. Wjiat is proposed in its place? As I understand it, that is the only piece of legislation on the statute books which pertains to cooperatives as a whole. If it is taken off the statute books what is to be put in its place? What shall we be left with? That is my question.
I hope the Acting Minister of Finance will be able to tell us to-day, or in the near future, that he is bringing down, or that the government is contemplating bringing down, a dominion cooperative act, so that in the future cooperatives will have something to lean on, something to guide them and to show them when they are right or when they are wrong. Much of the controversy over this question in the last few years arose from the fact that there was nothing on the statute books definite enough to guide the cooperative movement. In fact had it not been for the indefiniteness of section 4 (p) it is possible we would not be considering these matters today. As I have said, if in the near future the government will bring down a dominion cooperatives act setting out clearly the definition of a cooperative, and making definite provisions in the tax law for cooperatives as such, we shall save ourselves a great deal of trouble.
When we examine closely resolution 12 we find it does not provide, nor does it contemplate providing, anything for cooperatives as such. It refers to certain companies and to taxpayers, but after section 4 (p) has been repealed there will be nothing to provide for cooperatives as such. In other words the effect of the whole thing, as I see it, will be to place cooperative enterprise in such a position that it will be drowned or immersed in private enterprise. There will be no cooperative enterprise recognized as such. The very fact that the section is to be repealed, and that the resolution as it stands to-day, even with the amendments, is so vague, shows that the government evidently has not taken into consideration the enacting of a dominion cooperatives act, which would be something upon which cooperatives could depend.

Hon. members, particularly hon. members of the C.C.F. have taken a position that is surprising to me, that what we are proposing constitutes an attack on cooperatives.

Then, at page 3593 he returned to that subject and said:
I must say that we have tried to be so fair to cooperatives in this matter that I have been a little surprised at the fury of the attack of some members of the C.C.F. on our motives and on our acts in this regard.
I can hardly agree that there was fury in our attack. There may have been a little forceful language, but I do not think we exhibited actual fury. The point I would bring out is that what we have said in the house and what we are doing now is not something undertaken because w'e want to cause controversy. What we are trying to do is to reflect the feelings of cooperatives themselves. In order to establish that, I wish to read from advertising or a directive appearing in an issue of the Manitoba Cooperator of July 19, 1946. The heading in large letters is "Act Now", and it goes on to say:
The whole subject of budget proposals on the taxation of cooperatives is a serious matter. If strong action is not now taken it may be seriously regretted in the near future. Members of cooperative organizations have their opportunity now to stick together to protect themselves in the present crisis.
These are strong words.
It is a struggle to keep discriminatory and arbitrary legislation off the books. Let Ottawa know that you do not want this legislation. It is vicious. Act now.
This is not C.C.F. propaganda; this is the cooperator speaking. I could quote from various publications in the last few weeks in which it is indicated that the cooperatives have reacted violently to the proposals brought down in the budget.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: In fairness I think it should be said that I do not think they fully understood them.

I am glad the government has gone to the extent of offering the amendments placed before us to-day. They do not satisfy all the demands. They go part of the way. As a matter of fact I had an amendment drawn up which I would have presented had I been given an opportunity. If as time develops we find that the amendments now proposed are not what they appear to be, we mar^ still have to present our amendment.
When the minister said in his speech that he was leaning over backward in order to be fair to the cooperatives there must have been something wrong somewhere. The cooperatives immediately and spontaneously rejected the proposal. In the brief time between the presentation of the budget and the present debate the government found it necessary to

change its policy. I know the acting Minister of Finance tried to make it appear that it was not a change in fundamental policy, but-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I did not try to give that impression at all. I said frankly that following the representations which had) been made we had decided to make these changes. I think there is one change which is certainly fundamental in character from the findings of the MoDougall commission report, that is the different treatment given to members and non-members. I do not want it said that I tried to make it appear that there was no change in policy.
'Mr. ZAPLITNY: Perhaps I was wrong, but that is the way it appeared to me. The acting minister apparently was not quite willing to accept the statement of the leader of the apposition that this was back-pedalling in policy.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I never like such terms as back-pedalling. I am always willing to change my mind when I hear representations which convince me that they are well founded.

I congratulate the acting minister upon that attitude because I think that is the proper way to look at it. I think w'e should recall what were the objections of the cooperatives, in order that we may have a background upon which to decide whether the concessions made are sufficient to satisfy those objections. I should like to put on the record something which has been put on already in bits here and there. These are five objections to the proposals, made by the Manitoba federation of agriculture and cooperation, which I believe speaks at least for all the Manitoba cooperatives. From the telegrams and letters I have received from other provinces I think substantially the same objections have been taken there. I quote:
1.	Proposals ignore basic differences between cooperative and private business.
2.	They force cooperatives to treat members and non-members alike in respect to patronage dividends. This would eventually destroy cooperatives.
3.	Proposals prevent cooperatives from providing service at cost by forcing them to pay tax on three per cent of employed capital.
4.	They interfere with the right of the individual member to leave his earnings with his own cooperative by forcing payment in cash within six months.
5.	The proposals provide that the minister may in his discretion discriminate between cooperatives in the matter of retroactive taxation with the result that cooperatives do not yet mow their tax positions.
As I said, some of these objections have been overcome by the amendments, but taking the five objections as a whole I doubt whether if the cooperatives will acquiesce in what has

Income War Tax
been presented to-day. I do not think we should hold back on the demands that they have made. I should like to refer to one of the proposals which I think is ill-considered, that is the proposal to force-I do not know whether that word will be acceptable to the acting minister-the cooperatives to pay a profit of three per cent on the capital employed. I think I can establish what I have in mind.
Apart from the amount of money which will be involved, which I submit is a secondary consideration, the principle involved is that these cooperatives have organized on a cooperative basis; they have signified quite clearly that they do not believe in the opposite way of doing business, the private enterprise system. They organized their cooperatives to overcome the weaknesses in the other system and yet the government comes along and in effect says: You are going to become a good capitalist organization and like it. We are going to make you pay profits on the capital employed, or else you will be penalized for not doing it. This is a fundamental issue in this matter. Why should any government which prides itself on being a free enterprise government force any organization or any group of organizations to do business in a way in which they have signified they do not believe? The very fact that they have organized themselves into cooperatives shows that they have lost faith in the private enterprise system. Although this three per cent proposal ,is a small thing in itself, it serves to remind them that they are still living in a capitalist society and are to have capitalism shoved down their throats whether they like it or not. I object to that.
I believe there is room in a democratic society for all forms of enterprise. Whether we believe in one form or another is neither here nor there. At the present time there happens to be in office a government which believes in private enterprise. Well and good; but at the same time wye are living in a free economy, and we should permit cooperative associations to do business in the way they wish without interfering with their internal arrangements by saying: You must pay so much on the capital employed. I take strong objection to that, and I hope the proposal will be withdrawn before this discussion is over. The government seems to have overlooked the economic and social values of the cooperative movement as a whole.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Not at all.

This is not altogether a question of dollars and cents; it is primarily a matter of principles and values. There are more values in society than dollars and cents.
Earlier to-day we did hear something about how success can be measured, but I do not think it can be measured by the wealth accumulated. The cooperative movement in this country should be the pet of the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Finance told us the other day that there is still a great danger of inflation. It is in the interests of all who want to ward off inflation to promote the growth of the cooperative movement.
I should like to give some figures to show how the cooperative movement would help in preventing inflation. Inflation is not caused only by surplus money, although that erroneous impression has been left upon the minds of the people. They have been told that when they have too much money there is danger of inflation, but there is another factor that enters into the picture besides the surplus money over the amount of goods available. There is the urge to raise prices. You can have an abundance of money and a shortage of goods, but if there is no urge to raise the price of each unit you will not have inflation. Under the private enterprise system there is the urge to raise prices at every opportunty, because prices reflect income and profit. I am not saying that that is immoral, because at the present time it is probably the natural reaction under the economic system that is now operating; but there is that motive.
If goods are in short supply and money is plentiful, those who have goods to sell and who are in position to set the prices of the goods they sell will raise their prices as high as they can by letting people bid against each other in order to create an inflated price. But with a cooperative movement the situation is different. In a cooperative organization the customer is also the owner, and there is no motive for him to raise the price which he himself has to pay. The motive is service at cost. It does not matter what shortages there are or how plentiful money is; there is no incentive for a cooperative to raise prices against itself. For that reason the cooperative movement has a stabilizing effect on our economy.
Here are the figures I said I would give. In Sweden it is admitted that the cooperatives have risen to great heights. They have been effective in reducing the prices of the following commodities: The price of margarine has been reduced by 59-2 per cent; flour, in spite of the fact that the price of wheat went up, went down 11 per cent; rubber footwear, 58-8 per cent; linoleum, 15 per cent; electric light bulbs, 37 per cent; gasoline 55-4 per cent-it is too bad we did not have cooperation on the prairies last fall in the gasoline business when the price of gasoline was increased by two cents a gallon.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: Over what period did these decreases take place?

I have not the precise years. It was over a period of time. Silk fibre went down 50 per cent in price and superphosphates went down 15 per cent. That shows the effect which cooperatives can have on the whole economy if they organize to protect themselves from the high prices they would otherwise have to pay. I do not think the period has any particular bearing on this discussion, may I say in reply to the Minister of National Revenue. The fact that the cooperatives in Sweden have been able to reduce prices shows what a stabilizing effect they can have on the whole economy. For that reason I think the Minister of Finance should be very happy to do everything possible to promote the growth of cooperatives at this particular time.
Cooperatives have another economic value which is important, and that is in the prevention of the growth of monopolies and cartels. I have a clipping here from the Christian Science Monitor of July 17, 1946, in which certain figures which are illuminating are given in an editorial. It points out that fifty years ago there were 15,000 tobacco manufacturers; to-day there are less than 300. It goes on to say:
At the turn of the century there were nearly 700 iron and steel manufacturers; now there are fewer than 300. Manufacturers of lumber and lumber products numbered 28,000; now there are fewer than 12,000.
That shows the effect which monopolies have had on private business. The editorial goes on to say:
In another generation, unless the trend is reversed, there will be no opportunity for a businessman to enter any of the 100 or so basic industries in this country, except by the tolerance and patronage of the three or four companies controlling the entire industry.
If the government were to make a tax increase of two cents on the dollar everybody in the country would be up in arms, I am sure the minister will agree, but monopolies, through the very fact of controlling industries, can raise prices of commodities ten and fifteen per cent and, because we do not know just how and when it is done, we do nothing about it except complain. But the cooperatives do something about it. They do not just sit around and grouch. They organize themselves to give service at cost, and they prevent the growth of monopolies by giving the people of the community an opportunity to do business for themselves with themselves. That is an important function which the cooperative movement is performing.

I would urge those who express such great love for the free enterprise system, which to my mind began to die when capitalism was born, to do everything possible to preserve the cooperative movement and help it grow, be-eeause it is the surest way of giving everybody an opportunity to do business, whether it be called free enterprise or not. But if it gives everybody an equal opportunity and satisfies those who want free enterprise, I say they should support it.
I should like to quote from the Western Farm Leader, published in western Canada. In its issue of Friday, July 19, 1946, it gives some pretty strong advice to the government.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We get lots of that.

It says in an editorial:
By their failure to take into account the special social significance of the cooperative movement, the proposals respecting the taxation of cooperatives made by Mr. Ilsley in his budget speech reveal the reactionary trend of government policy. These proposals, if enacted into law, would remove, in certain important respects, the differentiation between cooperatives and profit-making enterprises which those who recognize the social value of cooperation have always properly stressed.
That brings me to the next point, the social value of the cooperatives. I have pointed out their economic value. From the social angle everybody will admit that the cooperative movement has done more than any other single agency to bring people together. This country of ours, made up of so many types of people, has been suffering and to a degree is still suffering from national disunity. There have been prejudices and divisions which have tended to divide the people and set them against each other when they should have been working together. The cooperative movement has, in my experience and in the experience of others, tended to bring people together on a common ground on the basis of self-help and for the good of the community. People of various religious beliefs and racial origins have been able to get together and work for the common good in an organization such as their local cooperative. The value of that cannot be overemphasized. It has also the educational value of giving every member an opportunity to know something about his own business. We are often told in this house that we should not discuss certain matters because we know nothing about them. If that were to prevent members from speaking, this would be a silent chamber. I maintain that through the cooperatives people have learned more about their business and what makes the clock tick in our economic system than they could have learned in any other way, because they are the owners of

Income War Tax
the business, the customers, the management and everything else in their own organization. In that way they see every side of the question.
It has been asked, what is the attitude of labour on the taxation of cooperatives? There are, unfortunately those in Canada who would like to drive a wedge between organized labour and the organized farmer. Most of the cooperatives in this country are in the hands of organized farmers. I have checked the magazines and other publications of organized labour carefully, also the news letters they send out, and I find that almost invariably the labour unions of this country have come out in favour of the cooperative movement and are protesting against the budget proposals to tax cooperatives. That, to my mind, is heartening, because it shows that organized labour has recognized in its own way the value of the cooperative movement in Canada.
I would suggest to the government that if they want to save themselves a good deal of grief they should give an opportunity to the members of this house to study this question a little further and, if necessary, let the item stand over for another day. The committee should perhaps be given an opportunity to study the various amendments which have been prepared by different members. I think it would be wise if these items were allowed to stand for further study in the light of all the proposed amendments rather than to try to carry on with just what the government has given us.
The last point I want to refer to is something which I do not particularly care to raise but which, under the circumstances, I am almost forced to mention. Listening the other day, and again to-day, to the leader of the opposition talking about the taxation of the cooperatives, I had to turn over in my mind and figure out just where the party which he leads actually stands on this question. I hope that he spoke for the whole group which he leads in this house, because it is commonly known that in the province of Manitoba the whole question of the taxation of cooperatives was started up and agitated by a gentleman who gives allegiance to the Progressive Conservative party and happens to be a Winnipeg member of the legislature. I refer, of course, to Mr. G. S. Thorvaldsen. I am not saying that, just because he happens to be a Progressive Conservative; all Progressive Conservatives are of the same opinion. I say that in order to clarify the matter, in order to make sure where we stand on this question, the leader of the opposition in this house-or someone else, if he wants to delegate to him that unpleasant job-
Nothing unpleasant about it.

should rise in his place and make dear the position of the party in relation to the stand taken by Mr. Thor-valdson. We have seen what has been done in the newspapers in the way of advertisements; we know of the issue of thousands of cards, signed in some cases by men who were not at the addresses given, urging us to tax the cooperatives. All that stemmed from the agitation started by the income tax payers' association. I am not objecting to the existence of the income tax payers' association. That is their business. They may have certain legitimate activities. But I say this-and I want to be very clear and plain on it-that I deplore the activities of that organization and of its leader, G. S. Thorvaldson, and the role they have played on this question. I do not think they have been fair. They have published much material which is questionable. In order that we may feel that the opposition, on this side at least, is united on the question, someone in the Progressive Conservative ranks should rise to-day and repudiate the stand made by the gentleman to whom I have referred.

speechtext:
May I say something in reply to the remarks made by the hon. member for Dauphin? I thank him for the objective and temperate presentation of his views; if he had not taken up the teaching profession he would have made a good lawyer.
I am not going to deal with the various points he has brought up concerning the desirability of cooperatives. Both the Minister of Finance and myself have tried to make it as clear as we could that the government is in favour of cooperatives and is not trying to discourage them; and on the last point he raised I think it is pretty obvious that we have not adopted the recommendations of the income tax payers' association.
The point I really want to make, however, is that it is difficult in drawing budget resolutions to be completely specific. The purpose of the resolutions is to indicate the broad, principle which the legislation to follow is intended to provide for and to permit a general discussion on those matters. Thus, when the specific legislation is brought before the house on second reading there may be criticism, and

There is just one other point I want to deal with, which was raised by my hon. friend, and that is the question of this three per cent return on capital. I think the minister, in his address, tried to make it perfectly clear that this is not an attempt to force cooperatives to pay interest or dividends when they want to operate on some other basis. But a great many cooperatives do pay interest and pay dividends now; a great many cooperatives, probably all, have certain employed capital, and it was felt that the capital earns some reasonable return and that that, therefore, could not be looked upon as a return from patronage.
I do not know that I could put it any better than the minister did in his speech as reported in Hansard at page 2921.
After careful consideration, the government has, therefore, come to the conclusion that it should accept the commission's recommendation that patronage dividends and similar payments be treated as a deduction from income subject to one relatively minor limitation designed to avoid at least some of the discriminatory effects I have mentioned. The limitation is this: that no company or association shall be able to go so far in its distribution of tax-free patronage dividends as to reduce its taxable income below a reasonable return on capital employed in the business. This reasonable return will be defined as three per cent on the capital employed, including borrowed capital, less the interest paid by the company or association on borrowed capital that is allowed as an expense in the computation of the taxpayer's income. The principle underlying this rule is that amounts set aside out of taxable income to be distributed in proportion to patronage by a cooperative or company which does not pay at least three per cent on the capital employed in its business contain earnings which arise from the employment of capital and ought not to escape tax entirely. For many cooperatives which pay patronage dividends this modification of the commission's recommendation will have little or no effect, for they already recognize an obligation to pay interest or dividends equal to at least three per cent on capital or retain undistributed income on which tax will be payable. Share capital with a limited dividend and -with limitation of voting to one share per member rather than one vote per share was a characteristic feature of the plan of organization of the Rochdale Equitable Pioneers Society, the

real founders of the cooperative movement. Cooperatives of this character will usually be able to claim the full amount of their cash patronage dividends as a deductible allowance. Any cooperative which does not set aside as taxable reserves or pay as interest or dividends a total amount equal to three per cent of capital employed, will find itself subject to tax on a portion of the amount it had set aside out of its income to distribute on the basis of patronage.

I would say at once that any association which makes a profit is not a cooperative to the extent that it does make a profit, and such an association should not be taxed on a profit basis like a private corporation. A true cooperative does not make a profit and therefore should not be taxable. Here is as simple and clear an example as I can give.
The head of a family spends $800 a year in buying groceries and general supplies for his family. He finds that a little too much and decides to join a cooperative in the hope that he will not have to pay out so much. At the end of a year, after joining the cooperative, he finds that he has still paid out $800 for groceries and supplies because the cooperative has sold at the same prices as anybody else. However, he finds that through his cooperative effort there is $100 coming to him as a patronage dividend. He has been buying goods from himself, so that $100 is not profits.

Not only were their profits exempt from taxation, but there was no hurry about returning them to members. Under an ingenious "revolving door" plan these profits were retained in the co-op treasury for varying periods up to seven years and usually at no interest.
That, thank heaven, is being removed. The writer goes on to tell with considerable glee that the cooperatives are going to be caught within another pair of pincers. He says:
Finance Minister Ilsley's new budget pro-losals, it is believed here, will end this era of iree and almost unlimited capital for the co-ops and will permit private competitors, if they wish, to meet the competition of paying untaxed patronage dividends to grain and other shippers.
Here is the next point, and this is the only point that is left:
For the private company shareholders, not to be confused with patrons or shippers who get the patronage dividends, there is also a little comfort in Mr. Ilsley's new proposals. Private companies have complained that payment of unlimited tax-free patronage dividends would allow a cooperative to return every bit of profit to shippers and if they were forced to meet this competition, there would be nothing left for the shareholders who subscribed the original capital. In other words, cooperatives could operate at no profit and private companies would have to do the same or lose all the business.
Mr. Usley now stipulates that no company or association shall be able to go so far in its distribution of tax-free patronage dividends as to reduce its taxable income below a reasonable return on capital employed.
That is the point upon which all discussion must hinge from now on. The minister has wiped out all other objections, and this is the only one remaining. I am arguing now that this is the moment to wipe this one out, but if the minister would like to have another day or two to consider it, all right. But this is the one that should be wiped out, not that it would mean a very great deal in taxation at the moment, but I regard it as the thin end of the wedge which will raise the cooperative movement off its foundations and tend toward its collapse. This is the beginning. I suppose
that this worthy tax payers' association which has been spending so much of its members'
. profits in trying to undermine the cooperatives in the last few years will be perfectly satisfied if it can get away with this much in the budget because it will represent the beginning.
Let me point out something to the minister which has perhaps escaped him. I want him to realize that the cooperative movement is not only a unit that operates in a community, but operates provincially and interprovincially. First, you have a local cooperative which serves the immediate community. That cooperative is affiliated with a provincial cooperative, and that provincial cooperative is affiliated with an interprovincial cooperative. Veiy well. Then as I understand this budget proposal, each one of them will have to set aside three per cent of its working capital and each one of them will be taxable. But it is likely that the capital would come from one source, largely from the local unit. They set aside three per cent of their capital and are taxed thirty per cent on that. Then it may be necessary to send that capital into the provincial organization, and the same demand is made there; again it is taxed another thirty per cent. Then the capital is sent to the interprovincial organization and taxed another thirty per cent. If this is not to be done I should like the minister to make that clear. If only one unit is to be taxed, the law would have to say which unit it is to be, or whether it is all three or none of them. As it stands now, each one of them is a cooperative, and each one of them must set aside a sum equal to three per cent of its capital, according to this proposal. Then it is taxable thirty per cent. It is true that the funds of the local unit have to be sent to its central provincial office to meet the demands there, and again it often has to be sent to the interprovincial office, so that it is important to have that point cleared up.
I have almost exhausted1 my time, Mr. Chairman. I shall have much more to say on this later, if the government does not consider the complete removal of this tax before it brings down its final legislation. I shall content myself now with pleading with the government to be as wise in consideration of the one remaining fragment of the proposal as it has been with respect to the others, and, if it is, not only will it do a great service to the cooperatives and thereby to this nation, it will indeed do a great service to itself.

I was absent from the chamber in a committee meeting at the time the minister made his proposals or the con-
Income War Tax

cessions which he has made, so that I am not any too sure of them, but I listened to the listing of them by the hon. member for Cariboo. It is perhaps a pity that the minister did not wait to make that statement until the end of the debate to-day, because a number of speeches had been prepared on the old formula. Therefore these members, had they made these speeches, would have been able to pat themselves on the back and feel that the concessions were made as a result of their representations. The minister has taken that joy away from them.
I want to make just a few remarks and ask one or two questions to clarify the budget resolutions in my own mind. I studied at some length the report of the royal commission; and, generally speaking, I thought the recommendations were sound and fair, fair both to the cooperative and to those people who consider themselves to be competitors of the cooperatives. The recommendations, I believe, generally speaking, received fair support from the cooperatives, at least far better support from the cooperatives than they did from the people who opposed them. I understand that the report was unanimous, and I think that is quite an achievement in view of the fact that one of the members of the commission was Mr. Arnason, who is, I understand, the deputy minister of cooperation in the government of Saskatchewan.
Whilst supporting, generally speaking, the recommendations of the royal commission, I did very much deplore the fact that the government had departed in several respects from the recommendations, and in every case where they had1 done so the departure was in favour of the opponents of the cooperatives rather than of the cooperatives themselves. I have received from my constituency quite a large number of telegrams, sent on behalf of several thousand people. The main points raised in these telegrams are as follows. First of all, they resented the fact that the government was proposing to treat members and non-members alike. I understand that that has been straightened out-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Right.

-and that the amount of patronage dividends which would have been distributed to non-members will now be taxable. I think that is quite just, because it means that the members would1 profit on the business of non-members, to which I do not think anybody can take exception.
Then, they charge that the proposals are a serious threat to the expansion of co-

operatives and will prevent the use of the revolving fund. Am I to understand that this has -also been taken care of?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Any net additions to the revolving fund are taxable, but the revolving fund continues to revolve.

Then, they protest the proposal to levy a tax on an amount equal to three per cent of the capital employed less interest thereon. I think that is, generally speaking, the provision, and I understand that that has not been wiped out. That, I think, is the main complaint, and I still cannot follow the minister's argument in trying to justify that being done, because, after all, this capital is the capital of the person who put it in; he paid income tax when he put it in, and he is going to pay income tax on any patronage dividends paid on that capital.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No. If dividends are paid on that capital that can be set off against the three per cent, if my hon. friend understands me.

No. I am not talking
about a cooperative having to pay an income tax on a patronage dividend; but the recipient of the patronage dividend will have to pay an income tax on that dividend if it is from a producer cooperative?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Right.
If it is from a consumer cooperative he will not?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is right.
No tax as far as the consumer cooperative is concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: So I am advised.

The only justification for the three per cent tax will be where the three per cent on capital represents business done with non-members. I mean to say, if the amount of the patronage dividend due but not paid to non-members is equal to three per cent, I do not think there can be any objection, because they will have to pay a tax on the dividends which have been paid to non-members, and therefore, if the grand total of that equals three per cent on capital, there will be no objection to that three per cent being taken. In many cases however, the non-members will be so few that the amount of their patronage dividends will not be equal to three per cent of the capital employed, but if there are a large number of non-members the amount of the dividends would be, or might be, more than three per cent of the capital employed.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Of course, if dividends are
paid to non-members-there is no obligation to pay them-they may be deducted from the gross income in just the same way as patronage dividends declared to members. In the case of the three per cent to which my hon. friend is referring, it is based on the assumption that the capital employed in the business earns a reasonable return, and that that return is not derived, in the case of the producer cooperative from the marketing of the primary products; in the case of the consumer cooperative, from the purchases made by the members of the cooperatives; but that the capital employed has actually earned a reasonable return, which it is suggested here should be three per cent, and that that should be considered as taxable income if the organization has not paid the equivalent of that amount to either shareholders who have shares in the form of dividends, or to lenders who have lent them money at a rate sufficient to absorb interest equivalent to three per cent on capital employed. That is all the provision is intended to accomplish. I do not know whether I have made myself clear. I should have added-or if it retains reserves which are subject to tax equivalent to that amount.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: STATEMENT OF ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE WITH REGARD TO GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
With the permission of the house, I wish to make a statement on the subject of gold mining. Since the restoration of the Canadian dollar to parity with the United States dollar, various suggestions have been made in this house for government action on behalf of this industry and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) and myself have received a number of suggestions and recommendations from persons and organizations outside the house. In this field where the possibilities of speculative profit or loss are so important we have so far, of course, given no indication or hint of what the government might do. However, I am now
in a position to state the results of the government's consideration of the various suggestions which have been made and of others which have occurred to us, and I now wish to announce them in this public statement so that all may have an equal opportunity to learn about them at the same time.
It is the case that one effect of the government's action in altering the exchange rate is that Canadian gold producers will receive approximately $35 instead of approximately $38.50 per ounce, Canadian funds. The change in the exchange rate has, of course, other effects bearing on the position of this industry. For example, this action will help to keep the cost of mining gold in Canada from rising, just as our whole stabilization programme has been protecting us from an undue rise in costs and prices during the past five years. Indeed, as the minister pointed out in his statement of July 5, the alternative to changing the exchange rate was to allow ' economic forces to work out an increase in our price and cost structure, more or less to the United States level plus ten per cent.
Four types of action have been suggested and the government has naturally given the most careful consideration to all of them. To deal first with the simplest and least important suggestion, it has been pointed out that the mint is making a charge for handling and marketing gold that exceeds the mint's out-of-pocket costs of performing the service. After considering this matter, we have come to the conclusion that we can reasonably reduce our handling charge from thirty-five cents an ounce to twenty cents an ounce, and the necessary instructions are being given to the mint to do so without delay.
The second matter is much more important and difficult. We have been requested to grant export licences for gold freely in order to permit our gold producers, and perhaps others in Canada, to sell gold to other countries at prices above $35 an ounce, which is the standard price of gold for monetary purposes. It is claimed that there are persons in various countries-India, Egypt, Greece, Mexico, Cuba and Argentina have been mentioned-willing to pay substantially higher prices for gold. As yet, no one has put forward specific proposals involving sales abroad which would be legal and for which United States dollars or equivalent foreign exchange could be obtained, although it is possible that some few opportunities of this kind might be found. We have made inquiries and we find that these alleged high prices are, generally speaking, expressed in terms of inconvertible paper currencies and that even if sales were effected at these prices it would be impossible to convert the proceeds
Gold Mining

into Canadian dollars. Our inquiries show there are very few, if any, markets where our gold could be legally sold at more than $35 per ounce for United States dollars or currency that could be converted into United States dollars. There are some private gold transactions taking place at premium prices in certain parts of the east, but most or all of the countries concerned are in the sterling area. We could not justify accepting payment in sterling for our gold1 production, and these countries would not be prepared to pay us in United States dollars, as they need their dollars for imports very much more essential than gold to be used merely for private hoarding. In regard to Mexico, the fact is that the Mexican government (or its central bank) buys from its own gold producers on the basis of $35 an ounce and itself obtains whatever profit can be made from sales above that price. Mexico is still exporting a good1 deal of gold at the standard price. Any imports of gold from Canada would require a licence and licences would not be granted unless the central bank itself wanted gold, for which it would pay on the basis of the standard price. In Argentina there is, apparently, a small free market for gold coins which are relatively scarce these days, but not for bullion. On the basis, therefore, of the information we have been able to obtain we have come to the conclusion that the vision of export markets at high prices is largely a will-o'-the-wisp and that no significant amount of Canadian gold could be legally sold abroad at premium prices unless payment were taken in an inconvertible local currency, which would be of no use to the Canadian seller.
Moreover, if we as one of the major producers of gold were to allow Canadian gold production to flow to these private markets, we would have to expect others to follow our example. If the output of American, South African and Australian mines as well as of our mines were allowed to flow to these private markets, how long would the price stay up-and, indeed, what country in which a premium price now prevails could afford the foreign exchange to permit the flow to continue? It is clear that a premium market for gold could not be expected for any sizeable quantity or for any considerable length of time. Competition would quickly bring the price down to the standard price. Indeed, the main reason why there are any prices above $35 an ounce is simply that there are restrictions outside of Canada on the export or import of gold or on securing foreign exchange to pay for it.
In any event, whether or not there are private hoarders willing and able legally to 
buy our gold for dollars above the standard price, we are convinced that we can best assure a satisfactory long-run market for our gold by avoiding these speculative export markets and continuing to regard gold as an international money, used for settling balances between countries. It is this fundamental, and quite sensible, use of gold which really gives it its value and which assures a steady, unlimited market for it at an established price. We believe that for us to go shipping our gold off to private hoarders and speculators in various hole-and-corner markets of the world might, over the long run, prejudice the position of gold for international monetary purposes and the various national and international arrangements affecting it. I think we would all agree that it would not be in the best interests of the gold mining industry to take any action which might endanger what must in any case be the major market for our gold and the underlying support of its price.
For the reasons I have given, we are not prepared to grant licences for the private export of gold, except in the normal types of circumstances where licences have been granted in recent years, for example, for the export of ores which require smelting before refining.
We have also been asked about the sale of gold within Canada. Under an understanding reached a number of years ago, the gold mines, with the exception of a few mines the ores of which require treatment by smelting before they can be refined by the mint, have been selling all their gold to the mint. This arrangement we believe is desirable and should be continued. We see no reason to encourage the private hoarding of gold. It would serve no useful purpose, but would, on the contrary, reduce the amounts available for the only sensible non-industrial use of gold, namely, the settlement of international balances. Moreover, the industry itself would suffer if the existence of a Canadian gold market were to make it easier for highgraders to carry on their illegal operations.
I come now to the fourth suggestion, which relates to the depletion allowance for gold mining companies and the shareholders of such companies. It has been recommended by various persons and organizations in the mining industry that the present depletion allowances of 33^ per cent to the corporation and 20 per cent to the individual shareholder should be increased to 50 per cent in each case. The principal argument advanced by those who advocate creating this large segment of tax-free income is simply that the gold mining industry has not continued to expand as rapidly as they think desirable, that few successful new mines have been found in recent years,

Gold Mining
that consequently taxation must be to blame and that we should, therefore, reduce tax liability in this way in order to create highly attractive prizes that would tempt new capital and enterprise into this hazardous but important field.
The difficulty with this type of approach is that it would give relief where it is not needed and no effective relief where it is needed. It would increase substantially the non-taxed income of the more profitable mines but it would be of no help at all or very little help to the marginal mines. Already under the present law successful mining companies are able to get a return of, and an adequate return on, their capital invested in resources that are subject to depletion without the return of capital being subject to tax, and the shareholders of these companies receive a portion of their dividends tax-free, as it is deemed to be return of their capital. To increase to 50 per cent the depletion allowance for these highly successful enterprises where the company and shareholders are already receiving, or have already received, their capital back tax-free, would be to single out certain incomes-many of them quite high incomes-for particularly favourable treatment that would seem impossible to justify on any grounds of logic or equity. If a subsidy for gold mining were really needed and desirable in the country's interest, it should be possible to devise a more equitable and effective subsidization plan than one which gives most to those who need it least. The government, therefore, finds itself unable to accept this recommendation.
However, it has canvassed the possibility of modifying the arrangements relating to depletion allowances in such a way as to benefit marginal mines, those which by reason of low grade ore or insufficient ore or high cost of production make small profits or are likely to make profits for only a short period. Under the present arrangements such mines may not get all their depletable capital back through the allowance because their profits are too small or the working life of the mine too short to return as depletion the total capital amount involved. It is these marginal mines which have the best case for some change in the depletion allowance, although I should mention, in passing, that of course they will also benefit most from the holding down of costs which the new exchange rate makes possible.
In view of all the circumstances, the government has decided to modify as a temporary measure its present formula for the determination of depletion allowances in respect of gold mining companies in such a way as to assure a minimum depletion allowance of two dollars per ounce of gold produced. In other words, 63260-249
a company engaged in the mining of gold will in respect of its first two fiscal years ending after June 30, 1946, be allowed the option of accepting as depletion either 33j per cent of net profits or $2 per ounce of gold produced, whichever is the greater. This will be of assistance to the marginal mines which really need assistance, but will not benefit the highly profitable mines which already do well on the present depletion formula.
Before concluding these remarks I wish to announce an additional measure which relates to the budget proposals of this year and which should be of encouragement to the whole mining industry. The house will recall that in the recent budget the Minister of Finance proposed that new mines coming into production after January 1, 1947, would pay only half rate corporation income tax on their profits of the first three years of production. When this resolution is before committee an amendment will be moved to change this provision for a half rate to complete exemption. This should give further encouragement to prospecting for and development of new properties and tend to offset to some extent the effect in this connection of the lowered proceeds or export sales of gold and other metals.

I will repeat what I said when Mr. Speaker was in the chair. I am in the hands of the committee. If there is a desire to discuss the statement which I made this evening with respect to the gold mining industry, I shall be glad to let resolution 12 stand and call resolution 30. As I said before,
