perhaps hon. members would like to consider the statement and 1 can call it early next week.

Before we proceed to make that change, I think the hon. member for Acadia should be permitted1 to finish his speech. I think I should put the amendment to the committee. I have read ithe amendment but I think I should now ask all those in favour of the amendment to say "aye."
What amendment?
The amendment moved by the minister when we came to resolution 12.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not want to insist that the amendment be put, because probably a good many hon. members would like to speak to the amendment. The hon. member for Acadia was speaking when the committee rose at six o'clock. The amendment had been read and, if the committee cares to proceed in the same way, that is quite satisfactory so far as I am concerned.

When the committee rose at six o'clock I was suggesting that if the volume of non-member business was large and patronage dividends were not paid out and were therefore taxable, the three per :ent proviso would have little or no effect lpon that particular cooperative. However, I ;hink the minister will agree that that would lot be a healthy state of affairs for a cooperative, and we should not encourage any such action which would tend to nullify the education work being done by cooperatives.
Just when does a customer become a member of a cooperative and when would the dividend be taxable or not taxable? The reason I ask that question is that there is a general practice among cooperatives to apply the amount of the dividend which would be paid to a non-member to his membership fee. I should like to quote from a letter sent out by one of the prominent cooperatives in the west to illustrate this practice, and in doing so I will not give the name of the cooperative. The letter reads:
Our records for the fiscal year ending October 31. 1945, show that you have done $81.65 worth of business. The rate of dividend has been set at four per cent, so that the amount of patronage dividend due you on your business is $3.27.
As has been the practice in previous years only paid-up members are entitled to receive dividends. All those doing business with us and wishing to receive dividends are being made permanent members. Fee for permanent membership is $5. Our records show there is $4.75 due on your permanent membership fee. This amount will be deducted from dividends.
When does that individual become a member? Would it be at the time the twenty-five cents was credited against his membership fee, or would he have to wait until the full membership was paid?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I think that would depend upon the by-laws of the cooperative. As my hon. friend knows, a patronage dividend, whether paid to a member or a non-member, is deductible from gross income. There is no difference as to the tax-exempt feature, if I may use that term, of the patronage dividend, whether it is paid to a member or a nonmember. I think the question of when a man would become a member of a cooperative would depend upon the by-laws or other internal regulations of the cooperatives.
I was thinking that if a dividend is credited against dues of a nonmember, then the association would be taxable.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It would not be taxable; there is no difference.

It was suggested this afternoon that the three per cent proviso is really the only objectionable feature left, but personally I am not so sure about that. The three per cent proviso is certainly a bad one. I say that because the government is trying by legislation to define a cooperative as a profitmaking institution. I consider it a vicious practice to define it as a profit-making institution. The minister shakes his head, but that is what it amounts to.
The point I disagree with most of all is in relation to the revolving fund. The majority of telegrams that I have received have referred to the revolving fund. I will quote one:
Budget proposals constitute serious threat to expansion of cooperatives. Taxing of revolving dividends will impede growth.
The minister, in his reply this afternoon, stated, and I got this from Hansard to make sure I have it right:
Any net additions to the revolving fund are taxable but the revolving fund continues to revolve.
He ended there. He might have added, until it is exhausted. The revolving fund accumulated in the past will not be taxed, but any additions to it will be taxed. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes, but it can keep turning over. Suppose there is $15,000 in it now. It can be maintained at that figure and keep turning over and over.

The practice is to pay out certain sums from the revolving fund from time to time, but if any new money is put into the revolving fund it will be taxable?
Income War Tax

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
It would1 have been clearer
if I had said that the net additions to the revolving fund are taxable.
Are we to understand that if a certain amount is paid out of the revolving fund and a certain amount of new capital is put in, that new capital will be taxable?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Not unless it increases the fund.
Then it will not be possible to expand the business without paying the tax?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is right. The expansion of the revolving fund will have to be made either out of patronage dividends received by the member and put back into the business, or out of profits-I call them, profits-which are kept in the business and would have to be considered as taxable profits. You cannot further build up working capital out of tax-exempt income.

If only part of the fund is paid out and a certain part of the patronage dividends is allocated or credited to the customer and made exigible and is put into the revolving fund, and there is an increase in the amount in the revolving fund, will that dividend be taxable?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The answer to that is this. If a patronage dividend is declared to member A, and it is $25, and it is desired that SIX) of that should stay in the cooperative and form part of what we refer to as the revolving fund, that could be done in two ways. A cheque could be issued to the member of the cooperative for the $25 and he would hand $10 back, or he could direct the cooperative to pay him $15 and keep the $10. It is just a matter of machinery.

The minister will note in the recommendations of the commission, section VI, that paragraph (3) reads as follows:
That cooperative associations and organizations, joint stock companies, partnerships, and other bodies and persons shall be allowed to deduct, in computing taxable income, such amounts as patronage bonuses, patronage dividends, refunds of excess handling charges, discounts, rebates and other similar amounts which are paid-
Not paid out by cheque at all.
-or credited to their customers, in proportion to the quantity, quality or value of goods acquired, marketed, or sold or services rendered; provided that:
(a)such amounts are paid in cash or its equivalent within six months after the annual meeting of the relevant fiscal period of the association, organization or company and within six months after the end of the relevant fiscal period of other businesses; or-

And this is the point:
-alternatively, that they are credited within the same period to each customer and exigible by him on giving such notice as may be deemed reasonable.
That is the recommendation of the royal commission, that patronage dividends credited, made exigible, should not be taxable. The same applies in Great Britain. I quote from page 226 of the report:
Again, in Britain, societies are financed in great measure by share or loan capital. Much of this capital is accumulated by crediting purchase bonuses to the share or loan account of the individual member. Payment for shares or loans is typically exigible by the individual member on demand or short notice. Accordingly, any patronage payment credited to the share or loan capital account of the member, or prospective member, may be treated as equivalent to a cash payment and is not taxed as income of the society. As old members withdraw and new members enter, the capital of the society may be "revolved" by means of patronage allotments by the society without payment of income tax.
That is the practice in Great Britain, and the comimission recommend that it should be the practice in this country. Therefore I cannot see why the minister insists that the money must be actually paid out to the member and the member return the money to the society. Surely, if the patronage dividend is credited to the member, made exigible, there should be no tax on the society. I would agree that the money of the customer would be taxable as the income of the customer if paid bv a producer cooperative, but it should not be taxed again as the income of the society. Otherwise you would have double taxation, thirty per cent on the cooperative, and then later the individual would have to pay a tax as well when the dividend is paid out to him. That is a vicious departure from the commission's recommendation and also different from the policy in Great Britain.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I am advised that there is no real departure from the commission's recommendation. This is a complicated matter and I do not know that I shall be able to make it entirely clear. It was found under our system there would be serious administrative difficulties if it were credited without any direction on the part of the member who would ordinarily receive it. Therefore it was decided that it could be paid in cash or its equivalent. If a dividend is declared and a portion is paid in cash and the balance retained on the specific direction of the member, the whole can be deducted. My hon. friend will notice that on pages 44 and 45 of the report under the heading, "Summary of Recommendations", there is a further provision that even if the dividend is held by the

Income War Tax
cooperative without the direction of the member in the way I have indicated it can be claimed as a deduction when paid out. I am advised by the departmental officials who have studied this matter carefully that substantially the recommendation of the commission in that respect has been carried into effect. I accept that statement. Perhaps my non. friend, like myself, finds this a little difficult to follow. Of course, as I said this afternoon, the resolution is only in very general terms, and even after the legislation is passed there will have to be the usual administrative practices to supplement it.

I would agree that it is certainly better than it was before the minister made his statement this afternoon. But where the dividends are credited or allocated and made exigible, there should be no question of the tax being paid, even though in later years it may be deducted.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: In the meantime they will nave to pay a tax, apparently.
There is one other point I should like the minister to explain to the committee if he is prepared to do so at this time; just what is the situation now regarding the wheat pools?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I made a statement on that this afternoon, so that perhaps my hon. friend would look at it.
I want a little more clarification. I understood the minister to say that the revolving funds were not taxable unless they increased.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Unless there was a net in crease.
Above what? What is the measuring stick by which you calculate the increase?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
From the previous year. Suppose the revolving fund at the end of 1946 were S25,000; that revolving fund could continue through 1947 at $25,000; but if it had increased to $35,000 at the end of 1947 I take it that the net increase, $10,000, would be considered as taxable income in that year. Does that answer the hon. member's question?
Mr. BENTLEY; I thank the minister for the explanation, but that does not satisfy me that it is a proper thing to do, for this reason. Supposing a cooperative agrees at the annual meeting by vote of the members that it will deduct each year from the dividends payable, say 12J per cent-some use 50 per cent-not a net amount but a percentage of the dividends. That amount of business in a certain
year will make 12i per cent of that, a certain amount of money. In the following year, through increased efficiency because of reduced costs, or more business, the amount may possibly be increased. At the end of four or five years, when the first amount has revolved, the actual amount of that revolving fund may have changed several times. Each time the business is increased, through increased efficiency because of reduced costs, or more business, and the same percentage is retained in the revolving fund, the amount of the revolving fund is increased because of that increased efficiency or increase in business, and you plan to tax them for having done that. I do not quite follow how you reason out the excuse for doing that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am not entirely sure that I follow my hon. friend correctly, but I assume from what he has said that the net increase to which he is referring is, in fact, income of the cooperative which has not been disbursed to its members.
Naturally, because it has been retained under agreement by them at the annual meeting. So I say that it is not a net increase that should be taxed.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That, of course, is a matter of opinion. I appreciate that my hon. friend thinks it should not be taxed, and I think it should.
But it is your intention to tax it?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is right, yes.

I am not going to deal with this question of profit-making enterprise from the point of view of either private enterprise or cooperative enterprise, but as I sat and listened to the hon. member who last spoke with regard to the increase of this revolving fund I wondered where that increase was coming from if it were not coming from profits. If it were coming from profits I think it should be taxed, and I believe that is the intention. With that in mind, I am going to ask the minister three simple questions. I have written them out so as to place them before him to make it very easy for him.
The first question is, has an estimate been made as to the annual cost or loss to the income tax division by the permission being granted to cooperative enterprises to deduct patronage dividends from their income tax returns? If so, is the minister prepared to state this cost?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The answer is that no such estimate has been made.

Would it be fair for me to estimate that it will run into many millions of dollars?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Or does it prove it if
you do?

I leave it in the air, the same
as you often do.
Next, if cooperative enterprises are permitted to deduct so-called patronage dividends from their income tax returns, will the same permission apply to those engaged in private enterprise who wish to pay yearly patronage dividends to those who assist, by loans or otherwise, in promoting taxpayers' business?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Well, as my hon. friend
knows, under the proposals private concerns may pay patronage dividends on the same basis as cooperatives, provided that they are paid in proportion to patronage. The main difference in the case of the private concern will be that the private concern must pay to all customers on the same basis. The cooperatives may pay to members and not to non-members.

I should like to enlarge a
little on the last reply made by the minister. I am to take it for granted from his reply that as a business man I am permitted every Christmas or at some time in the year to send out a cheque to all known customers doing business with me, and thus to pay out the entire profit which I might make during that year.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Good idea.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Only if, as provided in
the terms of the resolution, you have held out the prospect to them that they will receive that patronage dividend at Christmas or some other appropriate date.
We could very well do that. We could very well have done it in the last six years to the extent of our excess profit tax.
Some of them did it.

I am not one of those who did it. I should like it on record as to whether we are allowed to do it.
The other and last question-and I feel it is a simple one for the minister-is this: could a merchant at present doing business, who reorganized his business into a cooperative mail order enterprise, selling stock or memberships at $10 a share, with a total capital of, say $200,000, and who did an annual business or turnover of $1,500,000 with a net profit of 
$400,000, deduct this full amount from income return, provided that it was paid out in the form of patronage dividends or business bonuses?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is a pretty complicated question. I think I shall have to consider it carefully when I see it in Hansard and give my hon. friend an answer a little bit later, if I may.
Then I may look forward to an answer.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I will give some kind of
answer.

I hope the minister will permit merchants to deduct at Christmas or any other appropriate season of the year the excess profits tax on the suit for which I have been charged. Speaking for one of the largest cooperatives in the Dominion of Canada, in the dairy industry, I have one simple question, and I, too, have written it out, so that I shall not waste as much time as some of those representing the poor down-trodden private interests. Where capital stock bears a fixed rate of interest, which rate is written into the rules of a cooperative and is set aside concurrently in a manner similar to any other operating charge, is this to be considered corporate income?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
No, it is deductible from
gross income for tax purposes.
Mr. TOWNLEY-SMITH:	To come back
to this revolving fund mentioned by the hon. member for Swift Current, the revolving fund is not taxable unless it increases; is that the intention?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
That is correct.
Mr. TOWNLEY-SMITH: Suppose they increased from $35,000 to $45,000 because patronage dividends were left in. Those dividends would not be taxable up to twelve months. That is also correct?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Put it the other way. They may be deducted if they are distributed within twelve months.
Mr. TOWNLEY-SMITH: If this revolving fund increases because of the patronage dividends which were left in for twelve months, on what ground would they be taxable?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I think the answer to that is this. Let us take a specific date. Let us take January 1, 1946. The revolving fund amounts to $20,000; in the course of 1946, by reason of the fact that patronage dividends

Income War Tax
are not paid out, it increases to $30,000. If, before December 31, 1947, patronage dividends to the extent of $10,000 are declared and paid out, they can be deducted from the earnings of the previous year. If they are not declared and paid but are left in, that means that there will be $10,000 of income subject to tax in that year. Of course they can be declared. The recipients can instruct the company to retain them in the company, and in that event they would continue to be deductible, as I pointed out a moment ago to the hon. member for Acadia.
In that event would the minister consider that an annual meeting recommendation would be sufficient to show that the member had given the cooperative authority to hold them?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No.
Must it be in writing?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No; I think it must be individual authorization on the part of the member himself, not a vote of the majority of the members, which, in fact, would be the annual meeting recommendation. In other words it would have to be individual action rather than corporate or association action.
Why does the minister require that provision; is he trying to limit the growth of the cooperatives?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Not a bit.
It will have that effect.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not agree with my hon. friend that it will. I say that we are doing it only to maintain some semblance of logic, propriety and fairness as between those concerns which operate as cooperatives and those vhich do not. In my opinion the legislation is such that it cannot handicap in any way a genuine cooperative enterprise.
Has the minister ever been a member of a cooperative? Has he ever worked for one or helped to build one?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I have never been a member, nor have I worked for one. I have seen a good many of them operate. We have them in Quebec; I have talked to a good many people who are members of and are interested in them, and that is my opinion for what it is worth. I know my hon. friend holds a different opinion. It is obviously a question on which opinions may differ.
The minister said that if the capital were increased the increase would be taxable. I have one illustration here.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I cannot agree with that statement as it stands. Perhaps my hon. friend will elaborate it.
I will elaborate by reading a telegram.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It would depend on the way in which capital was increased.

The telegram reads as follows:
Our programme of improved facilities is financed by the revolving reserve plan of deferred patronage dividend loans from members and loan from the Saskatchewan cooperative credit society. If budget proposals adopted will involve considerable embarrassment in plans for repayment.
There is no question but that many of the cooperatives depend on the allocation of patronage dividends which are left in to be used as capital. Is this going to affect them? Are these patronage dividends which are left in as capital to be taxed?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I can answer that in this way. They are not going to be taxed in the hands of the cooperative if the man who receives them or who is entitled to receive them says: "Keep that amount of money in the cooperative and pay it out when I demand it."
Mr. TOWNLEY-SMITH: He may leave it for a year if he wishes.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
He makes an investment in the cooperative. In many of our cooperatives in Quebec the members make an investment in the cooperative; they buy a share or they may lend the cooperative money. The capital is obtained in various ways. They may acquire their interest in the way that is mentioned by using a portion of their patronage dividends to supply that capital interest in the cooperative.
Mr. TOtWNLEY-SMITH: The statement has been made that these patronage dividends are taxable if they are kept by the association for more than twelve months.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: But not if they are declared as patronage dividends and actually, or constructively, paid to the member. That is the point I am trying to make, but I am afraid I have not made it too clear.
Provided that they were actually paid, would the cooperative have to send the cheque out?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
No. I said that was one way in which they might do it. But I gave an illustration of two ways in which it might be done. One would be for the cooperative to send out a cheque for $25 and the member
Income War Tax

would send back a cheque for $10. I said that another and equally legal and effective way would be for the cooperative to send out the cheque for $15 and keep $10, provided that they had received the specific written direction from' the member to keep that $10.
He could receive a share for that $10?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes.
If the cooperative announced that they were withholding a certain amount, and it was an equitable amount, would that be satisfactory without having to get authorization?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Put it in this way. If the patron has his individual, legal right established to receive $25, which I used as an example, he is perfectly free to say, "Keep $10. $15 or $20, or even the whole $25 and apply it in the purchase of a share or keep it as a loan," or in any way he sees fit to furnish capital to the cooperative of which he is a patron or a member.
That could be done in the case of milk, a deduction of so much per pound of butter fat?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am advised1 that that could be done if there is a contract which authorizes the cooperative to do it on behalf of the members.
Is there not just one limitation to what the minister has just said in connection with the $25 which is kept by the cooperative on behalf of a member-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: And on his instructions.
Yes. If that results in a net increase in the revolving fund, does not that become taxable?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No. I realize that it is a little confusing, but the answer is definitely, no.
Does the tax legislation ignore the basic difference between cooperative and private business?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am afraid there was a little noise and I could not hear my hon. friend's question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If there could be more order in the committee it would not be necessary for the 'lion, member to speak any louder.
Does this proposed legislation ignore the basic difference between cooperative and private business?

speechtext: I would say no.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Does it do it?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The answer is still no.
Does it mean that cooperatives have to treat members and nonmembers alike?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No.
Are cooperative members allowed to leave their patronage dividends with their societies?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
If they so instruct the
society, yes.
I think it all adds up to this, that it will be pretty hard for the minister to bring in a bill which will cover all the statements he has made to-night.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is one point on which I am 100 per cent in agreement with my hon. friend.

I think this discussion has indicated the need for a cooperative act which will define what a cooperative is and make plain what the cooperatives are going to be up against. For instance, when the Minister of Finance was speaking on Thursday of last week he had this to say, at page 3593 of Hansard:
If this resolution that we are proposing as a result of the recommendations of the royal com-misison does not work well; if it turns out to be prejudicial to the development of cooperatives, which we do not want it to be, it can be changed.
I think the time to change it and make it right is now, and it would be a good idea if we let this resolution stand and had further conferences with the cooperatives themselves, and tried to make this legislation satisfactory all round.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I think, if I may say so to my hon. friend, that we shall make a little more progress along that line if, as I said this afternoon, the house sees the legislation that is to be brought in, and I question whether the matter would be very much further advanced by deferring action with respect to legislation until we have had further conferences with the cooperative organizations or others. There have been extensive conferences, as my hon. friend knows. This debate and the conferences we have had and the discussion that has gone on for a period of some years admirably illustrate the statement that it is impossible to please everybody, and I think we should make a start in this matter. As the Minister of Finance has said, and as I have said, we are following substantially the recom-

Income War Tax
mendations of the commission. I believe the proposals are sound, and I am also a believer in the process of trial and error. Let us get the legislation in force and see how it works. There are a great many people in this world who do a lot of crying before they are hurt, and I have a suspicion that that applies here. It may be, and I think is, due to lack of a full understanding of just how the thing will work; and I confess I could almost include myself in that class. Still I believe the proposals are sound. Certainly I do not feel that I would want to substitute my judgment for that of the commission which made this exhaustive investigation into this difficult question. I think the time to act in this matter is now. I believe we should get the bill into the house as soon as we can and let hon. members shoot at it, as I am sure some of them will; but let us try to get the thing settled.

I believe we are making pretty good headway here this evening. We had two big points to discuss and now, after a great deal of education on both sides, I think one of them is pretty well cleared up, at least until the legislation is brought in. I hope we shall not have to spend any more time in getting a clarification of the proposals in regard to the revolving fund. The minister's final explanation of that is quite satisfactory to me, provided that there is not in the legislation something which will change that around again. Of course, if there is, we shall have a whole lot more talking to do about it. The minister has suggested that he believes in trial and error. We do, too, and we have been trying this cooperative legislation without the three per cent which is now the difference between us. I suggest that the minister allow it to be carried on as it is, and that will be quite satisfactory over here. Perhaps the time spent in the house on the matter is costing the government more money than it will get from the three per cent provision.
I think we should realize that the cooperators are not making profits on people other than themselves, without being quite willing to pay income tax on any amount made in that way. That is a point some people fail to recognize. The sooner some of those who are throwing monkey-wrenches into the works realize that the cooperatives are not' profiting at the expense of anyone but themselves, that they are merely returning to themselves overcharges, the sooner we shall get along. So I suggest to the minister that he do away with this three per cent. It is not recommended by the commission and I do not think it works in
that way in the old country. If he will throw that aside, perhaps we can give him a clearance on this resolution.

I am sorry to come back to this revolving fund, but I do so because I think I can be helpful. The difference I see is a difference in principle; that is why I bring it up on the resolution rather than on the bill itself. Up to now the custom has been that at the annual meeting of the cooperative it is decided by a majority vote of the members present what amount shall be kept as a reserve, or a revolving fund, or whatever you wish to call it, and what amount shall be paid out in patronage dividends. I understand that system was satisfactory and there were no complaints from the members of the cooperatives themselves. If they did not like that system they could change it in their local cooperatives. The government now proposes to change that system by declaring that they cannot by a majority vote withhold any amount they wish, but that they must have an individual authorization from each member of the cooperative who receives a dividend.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: If my hon. friend will allow me, I take it he appreciates that the commission recommended against the practice he has been describing.
Yes, but that does not alter the argument. Regardless of what the commission may have said, we are legislating here for the cooperatives. The thing I am trying to get at-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
We are legislating for
Canada, not for the cooperators alone. We are legislating for every Canadian; I think that should be made clear.

Well, for the time being we are talking about the cooperatives as a group, and I am trying to point out that in effect we are telling the cooperatives how to run their business. We are interfering with the internal functions of the cooperatives themselves by telling them they must do it in a certain prescribed way. At the moment I am not criticizing the government for what they are doing; I shall do that later. I am only trying to find out what is the motive behind it, why they are doing it. There must be some particular reason why they have found it necessary to interfere with the internal methods of operating the business of the cooperatives.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The answer to that is very simple, if I may give it at once. We endeavour to treat every Canadian on the same basis as far as taxes are concerned. No other Canadian
Income War Tax

is entitled to build up capital out of tax-free income; and if the cooperative as such has income, it cannot be added to the capital without paying a tax on it. The commission recommended against it. We are telling the cooperatives how they should run their business in the same way as we are telling anybody else how they should run their business if they are or are not to be subject to taxation. That is all we are doing.

I am afraid that is only part of the story. I want the minister to understand that unless he is prepared to admit there is a basic difference between the setup of a cooperative enterprise and that of a private business, then we are at cross-purposes and we could argue all night. However, from the answer the minister gave to an hon. member who asked a question, I understood that he felt there was a basic difference. Maybe I should bring out that basic difference. In the case of the private business, where a dividend is to be declared the whole decision of how much shall be declared and when it will be paid is in the hands of the person who owns the business. The customers of that business have no say in when or how much of the dividends shall be distributed. In that case, therefore, it is necessary for the government to put a limit of six months, or twelve months, or whatever they like, in order to make sure that that dividend is paid, and not only declared.
If we wanted to take a hypothetical case we could say that if I were the owner of the business I could declare a dividend to my customers at the end of this year, but fail to pay it for the next fifty years. There would be nothing to make me pay it, because I am the owner of my business. No one can tell me what to do, because it is my money, even though I have declared it to somebody else.
But in the case of a cooperative that is not true, because the members of a cooperative are the customers. Therefore they themselves can decide when and how much shall be paid. It is, therefore, unnecessary in the case of a cooperative enterprise for us to butt in and tell them how to run their business.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
But the companies to which my hon. friend refers have to pay taxes on their profits, whether they pay dividends or not. The only difference is that the shareholder would not get dividends and have to pay taxes on them as personal income tax. However, the question which has been raised was considered by the commission, when at page 31 it says this:
On this first head of argument-

And the context explains what is meant by the "first head of argument."
-therefore, considerations of public interest do not lead us to the conclusion that cooperative associations should be given a blanket exemption from income tax while their competitors are subjected to the full burden of the current heavy rates. The considerations referred to do suggest, however, that where there is doubt as to what the income of an organization really is, the relative strength of cooperative associations and their competitors should be carefully considered to make certain that the solution finally adopted will not ruin one or the other, or unduly constrict their relative growth and development.
The granting of fiscal advantages is not usually a good method of giving special encouragement or assistance in the field of economic venture. Exemptions granted to one segment of the commercial community can scarcely benefit the public as a whole. Welcome though they may be to those who receive them, the burden from which some are relieved falls with proportionately increased weight on the rest of the economy.
It is for that reason I say that in drafting tax legislation one must see that it is fair to every Canadian.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Yesterday, while we were discussing another resolution, the minister made a statement which I warned I would quote back to him at the appropriate time. That moment has arrived. It was in connection with resolution 24 when, as recorded at page 3S70 of Hansard of July 25, the minister said:
It is believed that investment trusts of the sort being considered represent in effect merely collective investment by individuals, and it is considered' that the mere funnelling of income through the company to individuals should not bring on an extra tax.
I will admit that there are points of-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Substantial points of difference.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Yes, but also substantial points of similarity. The minister will correct me if I am wrong when I say that the granting of the exemption to these trusts, in respect of both corporation income tax and excess profits tax, was based upon the fact that the individuals who joined in this collective effort already pay, personally, a tax on what they earn.
That being so, I suggest that there is a substantial similarity in that the members of cooperatives are simply getting back a portion of their own income, on which they have already paid taxes.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: And when they do there is no tax payable by the cooperative. The patronage dividends are deductible.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The minister admits, by that, that there is merit and validity in the

Income War Tax
point we are making, namely that patronage dividends are savings and should not be taxed. That should apply all the way through, and that is why we contend the three per cent provision should not stand. That is our principal objection.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: On the so-called investment trust, under the funneling through idea, as my hon. friend knows the provision in our income tax law is that there will not be double taxation on corporation dividends. Dividends received by a Canadian corporation from another corporation are exempt from tax. In the case of the investment trust, the main point is that there is no active business enterprise carried on by the company. It simply holds the tokens, shares, or debentures of some other concern which carries on the active business operation. It is merely an intermediary, as it were; I wonder if I am expressing myself clearly; the so-called investment trust does not perform any active business operation. It is not a commercial corporation, as is a manufacturing company. It does not carry on active business, as does a cooperative, whether it be a consumer or producer cooperative. It is just a creature of the law, which holds the Stocks or the evidence of indebtedness of other corporate entities.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Very similar to the provincial cooperative set-up, or a provincial cooperative wholesale. I admitted, when the discussion began, that the analogy does not hold all the way through. Analogies are always risky. But the minister has said that the difference in respect of this investment trust is that it is not in the business of making profit for itself as a corporation. It is simply an intermediary, working in the interests of individuals who have put their money in there.
I submit that that is what we have in both producer and consumer cooperatives. We have the collective effort of a group of people, not to make profits but rather to save themselves money. As a matter of fact the case is much stronger for them than for those in the other examples mentioned.
While I am on my feet, I should like to say a word or two about one cooperative in particular. I do so simply because I am a member of it. I have been a member of the board of directors, and for that reason I know something about it. This particular cooperative is situated in Winnipeg.
What does it handle?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Chiefly fuel. It is known as the Red River Cooperative Supply Limited, and it is located in the area represented by the hon. member for Winnipeg South. One
feature I remember particularly about the first annual meeting of the Red River Cooperative Supply Limited was the enthusiasm and unanimity with which the members of that cooperative decided that, although the Manitoba law allowed them to declare interest on invested capital, they were not going to do so. That matter has come up from time to time since the cooperative was organized, and it has been declared the wish and desire of its members that no interest should be paid on their working capital.
This legislation opposes that principle.
The savings effected by the Red River company are paid out in dividends, and there is also a revolving-door fund plan which has been taking the place of extra share capital, which interested people subscribed in the early years of the organization. The people who buy their fuel from that cooperative are not making profits, as anyone can understand. They are simply saving some of the money which they have already earned as wages or salary, and upon which they have paid taxes. And as a matter of fact, because of the savings they effect in that way, these people are able to spend that money on other things.
I suggest to other sections of the business community that do not like the cooperative organizations to get stronger that actually it is better for the community as a whole to have these increased savings in the pockets of the people so that they can purchase other things. Not only is it a perfectly fair position that we are taking; it is a position much more farsighted than that taken by private enterprise in opposing the growth of the cooperative movement. It is the business of the government and certainly it is the business of this parliament to be interested in this movement, not only from the point of view of fairness and equity, but because in the long run it will be good for the community as a whole.
By contrast with this legislation I was interested a few days ago to read a Canadian Press dispatch from Wellington, New Zealand, headed "Consumers' Co-Op in New Zealand", and reading:
The latest step in the New Zealand Labour government's socialization programme is the introduction of consumers' cooperative societies to control all shops and other business in the huge state housing settlements being built throughout the country.
The proposal is that there should be communal ownership and control of all groceries, bakeries, butchers, hotels, theatres, restaurants, boarding houses, garages, service stations, coal, wood and milk supplies and any other consumer services required.

Is that from Russia?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
This is from New Zealand, one of the members of the British commonwealth, a sister dominion. The article continues:
Government officers have been canvassing state house tenants in the new suburbs for support for the plan. It is proposed to use state-built buildings which would be rented to the societies. Any profits would be distributed in consumers' dividends and rebates.
One society is already functioning at Naenae, near Wellington. No room for private enterprise remains in this suburb. All buildings are state-owned and are made available only to the society.
That is part of an effort by that government to improve conditions in all ways for the people by putting things more and more into their own hands. That is what the cooperative movement in this country is also seeking to do. The acting minister would like to have this resolution pass so that he could present the bill, but it is evident that the principle involved in this proposal meets with serious objection from those; of us who come from parts of the country where the cooperative movement is well established. If there were any validity yesterday to the minister's argument in connection with investment trust funds, there is much more validity to the argument that the savings of people which they save out of income and wages and on which they have already paid income tax should not again be taxed, not even to the extent of this three per cent of their employed capital.

Unfortunately, the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond is not in his seat at the moment. If he were I feel sure that he
would immediately correct an impression which the hon. member for Cumberland may have left on the minds of some hon. members. The statement made by the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond with respect to Doctor Coady was simply a statement as reported by the Canadian Press. I want to make it clear that he simply read a statement published in certain newspapers and attributed to Doctor Coady. I know the hon. member for Inverness, as I have heard 'him say on more than one occasion, holds Doctor Coady, as do all the members from Nova Scotia, in the highest possible esteem, and if the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond were here-

He is in his seat now.
He came in quickly when he was called.
I know he will speak in the highest possible terms of Doctor Coady.

Mr. Chairman, if I am in order, I should like to explain my position with regard to what I said in my speech on the budget dealing particularly with cooperatives. I spoke on that occasion while I was a member of and sympathizer with and militant worker on behalf of the credit union of cooperatives as I know them in my constituency. I was not familiar with all the intricacies and the policies and the philosophy of that particular movement, and on that occasion I did not express my own opinion but based my opinion of what was submitted in the budget on an announcement that was made by Doctor Coady as reported in the Canadian Press. As I read his statement, it was that Doctor Coady was very well satisfied with this part of the budget proposals dealing with cooperatives. Afterwards Doctor Coady wrote me a letter, which I should like to read in part:
A representative of the Canadian Press quoted me (Halifax Chronicle, June 28) as being thoroughly satisfied with the proposals of the budget resolutions on the taxation of cooperatives. There is no foundation for this. On the night that the budget was brought down, a Canadian Press representative called me on the telephone and asked me for my views. My answer was that I knew nothing about it. lie went on to outline the highlights on this matter and stated that patronage dividends were deductible before taxation, and that credit unions were to be entirely exempt. My answer was that if this were true it would be a triumph for the cooperatives. Subsequently it was plain that this supposition was not true. But the important "if" of my remark was omitted from the statement that appeared in the press.
He goes on to say:
I have now to say that legislation should be founded on sound basic principles. If not, it cannot long endure in a free society. The McDougall royal commission that thoroughly investigated this whole matter based their findings
Income War Tax

on a thorough understanding of cooperative principles, and brought in sane and reasonable recommendations.
Private profit business and cooperatives are specifically different kinds of business. It is logical to suspect, therefore, that no tax legislation that applies to the former would be applicable to the latter. Violence will have to be done to fundamental principles if this is tried. The essence of private profit business is that the business man takes a toll from his fellow human beings-legitimate in some cases, and positively unjust in other cases. In cooperatives on the other hand no member of the firm or company-to use the terminology of old-line business-can take a toll from his fellows. Any money he receives back in the shape of patronage dividends is his own money. These dividends are overcharges that were made by himself in the course of a year's business. By no stretch of the imagination, therefore, can patronage dividends be called profit or income. If governments want to tax farmers and labourers who engage in cooperative enterprises, they should do it under some other title.
As I said in my budget speech, I did not know anyone better qualified than Doctor Coady to quote in stating my position with regard to this legislation. 'Let me add that I undertook to ask the minister to-night questions which were put to me by members of the cooperative. I have asked three questions of the minister, and I understand from his answers that even the cooperatives themselves do not really understand1 this proposed legislation. I am banking on the authenticity of what the minister said. There is another question I will ask when the bill comes down.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services

May I add a little to the confusion? In the last fifteen minutes, from the opposite side of the house and from my right-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services

-I have heard a Liberal member and a Conservative member read a letter with which, apparently, they are in agreement, since both admit that there is

Mr. KNOWLES': He does not want to.

However, Mr. Chairman, what I rose to say-and I agree that this matter has been pretty well sifted and mixed up and I am still rather mixed up about it myself-is, that perhaps the focal point with regard to legislation on cooperatives in this budget is the matter of taxing that reserve fund. I am concerned about it for this reason, that I believe taxing
that reserve fund will definitely stop any further development of the cooperative movement.
Not if it is on a sound basis.

Maybe not. But I have been in this movement for a long time. speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That may be the case with consumer cooperatives.

I am thinking about consumer cooperatives now. If you are going to tax that overcharge which is given back to the member, and which he allocates back to that store for the purpose of promoting his business, what you are going to force cooperatives to do is to discontinue that overcharge-

speechtext: We do not do that.

-and cut their prices, cut down their units of business. Some of these stores have three or four thousand members. They cam cut down their units, distribute through the community, discontinue their overcharge, and run out of business the private merchant.

I honestly think my hon.

Do I understand that
when the bill is before the house the minister will be prepared to accept amendments and not take the position that, since the resolution is to govern the legislation that must follow, amendments in regard to particulars which are under discussion will not be accepted. What seems to be the fear of some of my colleagues is that once these resolutions are passed, the government may take the position, when the bills are down, that we must abide by the substance of the resolutions.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I would not take that stand, provided that the amendment being proposed by a private member were one which could properly be proposed by him. Obviously, if it is an amendment which can be proposed at this stage is could be proposed at that stage. Any amendment to the resolution which can be proposed, can be proposed when the bill is before the house and when it is in the committee stage. That is my understanding of proper parliamentary procedure.

The minister is not
closing the door?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No. I said this afternoon, of necessity, the resolutions are drafted in rather general and not too specific terms for the very purpose of allowing a general discussion on the particular principles of the legislation on which the bill is to be founded. I am not too clear as to the history of these budget resolutions. I know that from a constitutional point of view a resolution approved by the governor general must precede, a money bill; and in budget matters it is apparently the traditional practice to present a series of resolutions on which there is a general discussion. Then the government introduces legislation and there is further discussion on that. It has this merit, that it enables a good deal of general discussion to be held on the resolution stage, and in a good many cases it affords some guidance to the government as to what can usefully be included in the bill. Hon. members of the committee who have been here for some time know that, as a result of discussion in committee, very often numerous amendments are made to the legislation which is brought in. I think I can safely give the assurance to the committee that when the legislation is before us any amendment which can now be suggested could then be suggested; any amendment which a member, other than a member of the government, could properly place before the house can be made at that time. If there is any doubt on that point a record can be made of the passing of the resolution on division, for instance, which would indicate that there was not unanimous acceptance by some members of the resolution as it stands. I think that is a fair statement of the constitutional position.

That is a satisfactory statement up to this point. From the weight of opinion in this committee and from the discussion that has taken place on this resolution from all sides it is quite obvious that there is a desire so to amend the legislation that the cooperatives will not in any way be penalized or prevented from expanding as they should. What I have in mind is that some amendments which might be proposed could not be proposed by a private member.

I should like to assure the minister that I do not want to be any more persistent than any other hon. member, but I have been bombarded with telegrams from my constituents in Selkirk who believe that, under the legislation about to be brought down, their rights are being taken away from them. number of cooperatives do quite an appreciable business with non-members. I am sorry that the need for my presence in other places during the last few days puts me perhaps a little behind in this discussion. I am anxious that at some time, now or on second reading or at some other time, the minister should tell us what a cooperative is.
The second question I want to ask him is, what is profit? Until we know those two answers it seems to me we cannot advance very far.
However, here is my humble and simple thought. I live in the western country, from which comes the hon. member who spoke just a moment ago, who said to leave the cooperatives alone. Well, I wish we could, but if we leave them alone, the country will soon not collect anything in taxes, because everybody will adopt that method of doing business.
I am going to tell you, Mr. Chairman, what I think a cooperative is now. I think of a town forty miles from Calgary, where I lived, called Irricana, a very small village. On one side of the road was a grocery store run by an old friend of mine. He went broke and then died, though I do not suggest that going broke killed him. On the other side of the road another man had a store of about the same size. A dozen or so farmers in that area bought the store across the road. These were both general stores and their windows contained about the same things. Driving along in my motor car, granting that I did not know either one, I could glance at both and would go into the place whose window attracted me most. That is in no sense a cooperative; but persons calling themselves such have received consideration in taxation which the merchant on the other side of the street has not received. Mr. Chairman, before the resolution either in the original or the amended form is passed I wish to make one observation, and to ask one or two questions of the minister and, in the light of that, to try to summarize the discussion we have had this afternoon, so far as I understand it.
My observation has to do with the discussion we have had in the last few minutes regarding the reported attitude of Doctor Coady,
director of extension work at St. Francis Xavier university. I do this because I believe it was I the other day who questioned the statement of the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond. 1 wish to say that I do not think anyone in the house thought the hon. member intended to misrepresent the attitude of Doctor Coady. Then, I would ask the minister ito give an estimate of what the tax would be on those same three large cooperative organizations, the three western grain pools, in either one or dther of the last two years, on the basis which the government propose that they shall pay I do not mind saying why I am asking the question. First, he moved that the word "six" appearing in paragraph

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
If the hon. member had to wait to be told that, he is not half as intelligent as he appears.
With respect to my attitude on this matter, no member who is familiar with the history of the cooperatives in western Canada can have any doubt about it. Let me say briefly that if it had not been for the stand taken by myself and two other men-I happened to be
Income War Tax

premier of Manitoba at the time; another was the premier of Saskatchewan and the other was the premier of Alberta-if it had not been for our attitude with respect to saving the cooperatives from destruction in the year 1930 there would not be any western wheat pools to-day. At that time these well-intentioned organizations, trying to serve their farmer members who formed the organizations, had advanced initial payments on hundreds of thousands of bushels of wheat at a time when the price of wheat was rising. If I remember correctly the payments advanced were 60, 70, 80 and eventually 90 cents a bushel. I am just calling on my memory because this was in 1930.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: One dollar a bushel.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Macdonald says, "one dollar a bushel." The pools advanced that money to the farmers because the price of wheat was considerably higher, but before the crop was sold the price of wheat went down below the amount that had been advanced. These organizations, in order to finance, had borrowed from the banks, which was a legitimate business transaction, the way they were carrying on their business and had given the banks security on their organization for the repayment of the money. The banks saw the danger that was coming and they were taking the position that the grain should be sold before heavier losses were sustained. The three western premiers, feeling that, if a huge crop were dumped on the market, the price of wheat might be driven down to 30, 40 or SO cents a bushel, went to the banks and said: "Even though you have the power, do not do this. Do not do anything that will cause the market to crash. If now you want to protect yourself and you are afraid, we will guarantee that you will get back the money you lent to these organizations on condition that you undertake not to have this crop thrown on the market."
So the crop was not thrown on the market. The three western governments guaranteed the banks against loss of the money they had advanced to these cooperative organizations. But when the accounting came, the pools got less money for the crop than they had advanced. There were other steps taken, which I need not go into now, and eventually the dominion government was brought into the matter in later years. As I said, the pools had paid the farmers more money than they got for the crop, because in the meantime the price has gone down.
What was the result? I will deal with only one province. The Manitoba pools came into the possession of the Manitoba government

because of the guarantee it gave.. The Manitoba government could have kept these pool elevators. It could have sold them to private concerns. It could have sold them back to the farmers themselves. What did we do? We did not keep them ourselves. We had had in that province a previous experience with government-owned elevators which was not to the credit of government ownership, although I am not blaming government ownership generally. But the results in that particular case were far from satisfactory.
WTe did not sell the elevators to private concerns. Everybody was looking to get the elevators at a low price. We sold them back to the original owners-the farmers-on time. They had no money, but we had faith in their integrity, and we sold these elevators back to the men who had1 owned them before. We sold them back to them, not at the amount we had to pay to rescue them, but at a loss of one and a quarter million, dollars, and if the farmers of Manitoba to-day have a cooperative organization know as the Pool Elevator companies, it is because of that act.
While I am telling the story, let me say that the agreement entered into by that organization, as I remember it, was this. It was to pay for the elevators so much a year over twenty years. We had even to help them with their operating expenses. They have lived up not only to the spirit but to the letter of their agreement, and they now have those elevators practically all paid for.
The cooperatives in Manitoba never asked for any favour from me or from the government I led, and we never promised them any. But they expected, and we were always willing to assure them, that they would get a square deal. And now, as the hon. member for Calgary West has said, the job in this house to-day is to find a fair system of taxation of these and other organizations, to find it without discouraging or hurting these organizations, which, as so many members have said, are a splendid acquisition to the economic life of this country. I would not have referred to this personal experience of the past if it had not been for the question raised this afternoon by the hon. member for Dauphin. I do not ask this house to give favours to the pools. I agree with .those who say that we must find a system of taxation which by itself will not drive the industry of this country from one kind of economic industry to another. At the same time we must recognize what Doctor Coady said this afternoon, that the pools are not only a great economic organization but

a great social organization, and we in this house must not do anything to discourage their sound development.

While I support the
cooperatives I think it would be well that all the facts should be brought out, and if it is not going to tax too much our already overworked officials in the department I think it would be helpful if we had on the record the amount of taxes paid by the line elevators during the last five years and an estimate of the volume of business done by the line elevator companies in that period as compared with the volume of business done by the pools.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not think we can give the information for individual line elevators.

Could the minister tell us whether the legislation he has in mind as based on the resolution to be adopted will in any way differentiate between private business and cooperative business?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes, it will, more particularly with respect to non-member business. My hon. friend will appreciate that the legislation will have a differentiation in that respect.

The next question is
this. I understand that one of the first provisions of the resolution is that section 4 (p) of the Income War Tax Act will be repealed, although it does not say so in those terms?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is correct, and that is what the commission recommend.
Could the acting minister tell the committee briefly what are the chief reasons why it is proposed to repeal this legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The reasons are those given in the report of the McDougall commission and also given by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech, Hansard, page 2920, as follows:
The reasons for this recommendation-
That is, that section 4 (p) be repealed.
-are summarized in the report as follows:
"As a result of the ambiguities of language and the difficulty of administering the section, and because we are of the opinion there is no general class or group of cooperative associations in Canada to-day whose income should be declared not to be liable to taxation, we are of the opinion that the section in its present form cannot survive the attacks made upon it."

I am not quite satisfied with the reply I got a little while ago, and I also think it might be well if the hon. member for Calgary West had a little bit of a reply, so far as possible, given him to-night to his question. His question was, "What is a cooperative and what is a profit?" This resolution is important because it deals with those two very things.
All through our life in western Canada we were in the low income groups, mostly speaking. Every dollar we had to spend to provide for the needs of our families was important. We endeavoured to deal with the various dealers and concerns which we had to buy our goods from at the place of business where we thought we could get the best services or goods for the least amount of money. We found that this was not working as well as we should have liked. We had learned that in other countries, and even in other parts of Canada, there was a way of doing this, to save ourselves some money by buying collectively, because we felt there were too many middlemen between ue and the place where our goods were manufactured, or between us and the product of our labour from the farm and the place where it was finally put into consumable form, that we did not get our full share of the consumer's dollar for our wheat and meat and other farm products, and that we paid far more than the actual cost of manufacture of the goods we had to buy; that there were too many middlemen. Therefore we built these cooperative organizations so that we could pool our money in a collective way, to buy the goods we required with the least use of middlemen or speculators between the makers of these goods and ourselves. We did the same thing in building our marketing organizations. We endeavoured to build by the pooling of our money, not for the sake of interest on the money, but to put the money together to build marketing facilities and a machine which would take a little bit closer, under our own control, our grain and products to the people who were actually going to consume those goods.
That was our purpose. We tried a variety of methods in both the producer and con-
Income War Tax

sumer fields, and the dividing line is so thin that some day we may have to debate that point, but I will not do it to-night.
Earlier in the evening I asked the minister a question about the revolving-door fund and how it would be taxed, and when I had finished someone said that I was just as clear about it as the minister, and he did not understand a word. I said I appreciated the compliment. I am sorry if the minister did not understand what I meant, and I am going to try to make it clear to him. He stated that the intention is to tax any increase in a revolving fund. My question was, what place do you decide is the point above which is an increase? I drew up a little table here to show how a revolving fund works, and why I wanted this question answered, and how the minister might answer it.
I am going to assume that we started a cooperative, a consumer cooperative, if you like, in 1940. We operated that year. One man who had a good-sized family and ran a tractor bought his gasoline, drugs, hardware and groceries from that place, and the amount was a thousand dollars. I make it a thousand for the sake of the even figure. The patronage dividend declared at the end of the season was four per cent, which is $40, fifty per cent of which, by agreement with the cooperative is retained, in the revolving-door fund, to revolve back into his pocket after being employed for four years; that is, in the fifth year it would come back. So that in 1940 he put $20 into that reserve. In 1941 business was not quite so good, so that the dividend declared was not quite so high; it was three per cent on the same amount of goods bought by this man. Therefore the dividend at three per cent is $30, half of which stays in, namely, SIS, making $35 all told. In 1942, on the same amount of business, but because of fluctuations in cost of operation and so on, the dividend is 3J per cent; that is $35 on the $1,000, or $17.50 in the revolving fund.
Do you wish to call it eleven o'clock, Mr. Chairman?	.

speechtext: I wonder if the committee would allow my hon. friend to complete his example, so that I can have the week-end to look it over.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services

I gave the amount in 1942, $17.50. In 1943, the fourth year, the business in the cooperative has been a little better; that is, it has been more efficient in
TMr. Bentley.]
operation, or in some way the dividend is as high as it was in the first year; that is, four per cent again, or $40, fifty per cent of which, or $20, remains in the revolving fund. Added together, this means that in those four years this individual has in the fund $72.50.
Let us now understand the purpose of this fund. It is not for investment purposes; it is his share of the money necessary to provide the facilities and the machinery required to supply him with these goods and services from the shelf, out of the tank, or through the warehouse. He has already paid for these facilities with that. Having served their purpose, they then come back to him from the earnings of the next year, because in that year new members come in and should take a responsible share of financing their share of these facilities which are to serve them, because this is clearly a service organization.
In the fifth year, 1944, the dividends declared on the same amount of money are 4J per cent, which makes $45. That gives him $22.50. That would be a total of $95 that year. The first year, 1940, revolves, and therefore he gets $20 back. That leaves his fund $75. There has been a variation in the fund of $2.50. This year, having got the first year's back it is $2.50 higher, if my mathematics are correct. Does the minister get the point? It can vary from year to year according to the efficiency of the organization and the ability of the men they hire to operate it and buy the goods that they wish to buy collectively to put there. All the way along, because of the operations, they can increase or decrease the dividends, which will vary from year to year. The point I am getting at is, at what stage does the government's plan say the fund has reached a level from which an increase in the revolving fund is considered to have taken place for taxation purposes? Does the minister get the point?
